one_liner: Header-only mmap+SIMD std::cin/cout replacement, ~5x faster than libstdc++ iostream for competitive-programming I/O.
what_it_does: blazingio replaces std::cin/std::cout for competitive-programming judges, where reading and writing ints, floats, strings, std::complex, and std::bitset<N> dominates runtime. It exposes global blazingio::cin/cout objects with operator>>/<< that mimic iostream syntax, but they are not std::istream/ostream subclasses, so template code or manipulators that need the real types don't work. Rather than incremental buffered reads, it maps all of stdin into memory up front (mmap on Linux/macOS, mmap+ReadFile on Windows) before the first operation.
how_it_is_fast: It avoids libstdc++'s buffered streambuf and virtual-dispatch-heavy formatting entirely: the whole input is mmap'd once, then parsed and printed with hand-written SIMD kernels (AVX2, SSE4.1, or NEON -- picked at compile time -- with a scalar SWAR/bit-trick fallback) that scan for whitespace and convert digit or bitset runs a vector-width at a time. There's no locale handling, no exceptions, and no runtime CPU-feature dispatch, and formatting is restricted to fixed decimal, 12-digit-fraction output.
when_to_use: Competitive-programming/judge submissions (Codeforces, ejudge, etc.) where whole-program I/O time is scored and you control the entire source.
Heavy reading/writing of integers, floats, strings, std::complex<T>, or std::bitset<N> where sync_with_stdio(false) iostream is still the bottleneck.
Source-size-limited judges: copy-paste the pre-minified blazingio.min.hpp (single file, includes attribution link).
Target CPU's SIMD extension is known ahead of time -- x86_64/i386 with AVX2 or SSE4.1, or aarch64 with NEON.
You can tolerate UB on malformed input in exchange for maximum throughput on a single, short-lived process.
when_not_to_use: Any production or user-facing code -- the README explicitly warns invalid input can trigger UB 'including security vulnerabilities'.
Code needs real std::istream/ostream (templates, manipulators, locale, non-decimal bases, precision/width, exception-based error handling).
Need >1 ulp float accuracy or std's scientific notation for magnitudes below 1.
Multi-threaded I/O, or judges/hosts where the assumed SIMD extension might be absent (no runtime detection; wrong assumption is UB).
Very large output (roughly >0.5 GiB, or >24 MiB on old-style ejudge problems) may be truncated depending on the judge.

integration.form: header-only (ships a pre-generated single-file blazingio.min.hpp, plus a Python generator (minimize.py/common.py + config) to build custom platform/feature configurations)
integration.dependencies: none beyond the C++ standard library and platform headers (sys/mman.h, unistd.h on Linux/macOS; windows.h, io.h on Windows)
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (test.py compiles with -std=c++17); CI builds with g++, and also exercises clang/MSVC per repo workflows
integration.platforms: x86_64, i386 (AVX2 or SSE4.1 optional), aarch64 (NEON optional) on Linux/macOS/Windows; SIMD ISA is fixed at build time, no runtime CPU dispatch
integration.thread_safety: not documented; no mutex/atomic/thread_local found in source -- design targets single-threaded, single-pass whole-program I/O
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — matches operator>>/<< syntax for the types it supports (char, integers, float/double, std::string/string_view, std::complex<T>, std::bitset<N>, std::getline), but blazingio::cin/cout aren't std::istream/ostream, integers can't have a leading '+', only decimal formats parse, precision/width aren't handled, and failures are UB instead of setting failbit

gotchas: SIMD extension is chosen at compile time via the config file's architecture= list; running on a CPU lacking that extension is undefined behavior, not a graceful fallback.
No error handling beyond EOF detection (if (std::cin)); malformed input is UB, per the README's own security warning.
std::bitset<N> input requires at least N input characters -- std zero-pads shorter input, blazingio does not.
Output is capped at roughly 0.5 GiB generally, 24 MiB on old-style ejudge-based judges.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Only scnlib is a close analog (std::stringstream/sscanf replacement); scnlib returns errors and stays safe on bad input, making it viable in production, while blazingio is faster and cin/cout-syntax-compatible but explicitly UB-on-error and competitive-programming-only -- pick blazingio when you want near-zero code changes from std::cin/cout, need bitset/complex I/O, and can accept unsafe behavior for maximum throughput in a single-shot batch program. The JSON-serialization siblings (cjson.cpp, json.cpp, Cap'n Proto, etc.) solve a different problem (structured data, not whole-program scalar I/O) and aren't real alternatives.
verified_claims_summary: blazingio's own CI benchmarks it against std::cin/std::cout with sync_with_stdio(false) ('iostream_detached') on GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest x86_64 runners, g++ -std=c++17 -O2 (exact gcc version and CPU model not recorded). Across the 74 read/write test-and-mode pairs in benchmark-results/linux-x86_64.json (opened and spot-checked directly), per-test speedup ranges from about 1x (plain line input) to about 80x (bitset input), geomean about 4.7x; the README's headline '5x faster' figure describes typical integer/string I/O on Linux+libstdc++, with larger geomean speedups reported on macOS/libc++ (~22x) and Windows/MSVC (~15x) because those iostream implementations are slower.
status_note: Effectively unmaintained (last commit 2024-11-23, zero open issues, one trivial closed issue) but MIT-licensed, small when pre-minified, and self-contained enough to vendor as-is; usability is 'copy blazingio.min.hpp and go', not a library you'd integrate into a build system.
